consensus_summary: In apocalyptic contexts, beasts primarily symbolize brutal, God-opposing kingdoms, imperial systems, or their rulers; some readings also recognize Gentile peoples or morally bestial humanity.
book_summary: A beast signifies a worldly nation or kingdom as a predatory collective people; differing beasts signify differing kingdoms, while the unclean animals in Peter’s vision signify Gentile nations cleansed by God.
consensus_core_identification: Beast = hostile political kingdom, empire, or ruler.
book_core_identification: Beast = nation or kingdom generally, including Gentile peoples represented by unclean animals.
boundary_disagreement: The book removes hostility, oppression, and explicit opposition to God as defining conditions, extending beast symbolism from anti-God imperial powers to nations and kingdoms generally. It also incorporates Peter’s unclean animals as Gentile nations, a recognized but secondary consensus alternative.
material_contradiction: There is no central contradiction: both identify beasts with political peoples or kingdoms. The disagreement concerns scope and whether bestial imagery inherently denotes hostile or degraded rule.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus’s political-collective referent but broadens it beyond oppressive empires and rulers to nations or kingdoms as such. Its treatment of Acts 10 is not novel because Gentile peoples appeared among the listed alternatives, though the book makes that usage part of a unified general rule.
strongest_objection: Daniel 7:17 and Daniel 8:20–21 directly identify the animals as kings or political powers, but they do not establish that every symbolic beast means any nation generally. Acts 10 supports applying unclean-animal imagery to Gentile persons, yet does not explicitly call them nations or establish the book’s universal beast symbolism, predatory characterization, or contrast with trees.
